title: CPO Testing Faces A Moving Target Problem
gist: In an expert roundtable, Teradyne, Advantest, ISE Labs (ASE) and Keysight say co-packaged and near-packaged optics are moving into data centers before test is mature. There is no optical DFT, connectors and laser sources are not standardized, alignment tolerances are extreme, and CPO modules need 1-8 kW test power. The result is more test insertions, burn-in steps and automation demand in the near term.

insights.claim: Optical test lacks design-for-test, so each waveguide, ring and modulator must be tested one at a time, which is slow, laborious and does not scale, much like digital logic before scan test.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: Optical DFT is a white space, and until it exists CPO test time and cost stay high, a headwind to CPO cost-down.
insights.quote: We haven’t done DFT for optical.
insights.locator: Ira hit on an important point.

insights.claim: The main challenge in CPO test is scaling to high-volume manufacturing with production software, data analysis and automated optical alignment, not optical measurement itself, which transceiver makers have done for 20 years.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: ATE vendors with HVM optical automation such as Teradyne and Advantest could capture new test-cell spend.
insights.quote: The difference is the scale of going to high-volume manufacturing
insights.locator: Griffin: There are two key changes

insights.claim: Advantest views photonics as another step in ATE's progression from digital to analog, mixed-signal, RF and mmWave, but the optical test ecosystem is less mature and customers still have not settled on connection technologies or laser sources.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: Undecided standards delay volume test-equipment orders but expand eventual ATE content per device.
insights.quote: customers are still trying to determine which connection technologies they’re going to use and what laser sources they’re going to use

insights.claim: A shortage of hybrid engineers trained in both optics and electronics is a major bottleneck to CPO test.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: Talent scarcity slows CPO ramp and raises costs.
insights.quote: we don’t have a hybrid engineer
insights.locator: Ira hit on an important point.

insights.claim: Optical probe cards would be ideal but are hard because of non-contact mechanics and the need for optical calibration, and FAU unit-to-unit and channel-to-channel variation means small pitch or x,y offsets matter more than at electrical probe.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: Precision optical probing and calibration is a technical moat for test-equipment suppliers.
insights.quote: A slight offset due to pitch and x,y mismatch causes an optical alignment offset, which is more impactful than a similar offset at electrical probe.

insights.claim: The industry broadly sees five CPO test insertions (PIC, wafer-level optical engine, die-level optical engine, module, system-level), plus a wafer-level burn-in/stability bake that is a must for lasers to remove infant mortality.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: Multiple insertions per CPO device multiply test-equipment demand.
insights.quote: Insertion one is for PIC (photonics IC) testing.

insights.claim: Optical engine testing is a must and is where most of the effort goes, while some experienced players say PIC-level testing may not be needed in the future.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: Test spend may concentrate at optical-engine insertions.
insights.quote: Optical engine testing is a must, and that’s where most of the effort is.

insights.claim: A critical insertion comes before attaching optical engines to the high-value ASIC, so lower-cost optical engines do not cause yield loss on the entire expensive package.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: Known-good optical engine screening is economically essential, which secures that test-insertion demand.
insights.quote: you don’t want to package lower-cost optical engines with an extremely high-value ASIC and cause yield loss on that entire package

insights.claim: CPO module test requirements reach 1 to 8 kW for the center die and 10 to 30 W per optical engine, with 4 to 32 optical connectors per device, making thermal management critical.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: Extreme power and connector counts require new high-power test handlers and thermal solutions.
insights.quote: We’re seeing test requirements at 1 to 8 kW for the center die and 10 to 30 W for each optical engine.

insights.claim: Many CPO tests exist only because the ecosystem is immature and will go away as processes mature, but in the near term there will be more burn-in insertions, and DFT is needed to reach maturity.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: Near-term test intensity is elevated and may decline later, a cyclical consideration for test-equipment revenue.
insights.quote: But you will have more burn-in insertions because things are not optimized from a manufacturing and test standpoint.

insights.claim: CPO/NPO fundamental test parameters are largely the same as for optical transceivers; what changes is which insertion performs them and how early, and standards are being written in parallel with manufacturing test discussions.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: Existing optical test IP carries over, which favors incumbents with transceiver-test expertise.
insights.quote: What changes with CPO and NPO is which insertion performs them, and how early.

insights.claim: Package warpage in large CPO packages can misplace connectors so test connection mechanisms shear them off.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: Warpage is a yield and test risk for large AI packages, with demand for warpage-tolerant handling.
insights.quote: If you’re coming in with a connection mechanism and the part is warped, that connector is not going to be where you expect it to be, and you can shear the connector off.

insights.claim: A handful of customers will go to volume and drive specific connector designs over the next one to two years, which should determine which designs propagate.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: Connector standard winners should emerge by around 2028, so watch which connector suppliers get design wins.

insights.claim: There are predictions that FAU makers will not keep up with capacity demand, forcing second sourcing, which becomes messy if the second-source FAU uses a different connector type.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: FAU capacity is a potential CPO supply bottleneck and an opportunity for FAU makers.
insights.quote: there are predictions about FAU companies not being able to keep up with the capacity demands of the industry

insights.claim: Customers are discussing two-row fiber FAUs and hundreds of fibers in a single FAU, ramping faster than the industry has solved the last challenge.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: Fiber-count escalation raises complexity and content per CPO module.
insights.quote: We’re seeing customers talking about implementing hundreds of fibers in a single FAU.

insights.claim: Dust is the enemy in optical production test, so automated cleaning of the optical connector FAU is critical.
insights.speaker: Laura Peters
insights.so_what: Automated optical cleaning and inspection is a niche equipment opportunity in CPO HVM.
insights.quote: dust is the enemy in optical testing
